newsitem.title: USA: Jury sees new photos of Simpson in Bruno Maglis.
newsitem.headline: Jury sees new photos of Simpson in Bruno Maglis.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial on Monday were shown new photographs of him wearing the same kind of designer shoes experts say left bloody prints at the scene where his ex-wife and a friend were murdered.

Simpson has denied ever owning a pair of the Italian-made Bruno Magli shoes. The 30 new photographs were introduced by a lawyer for the plaintiffs during testimony by Robert Groden, a photographic analyst called by the defence to prove its claim that a previously introduced photograph of Simpson wearing Bruno Maglis was a fake.

As each new photograph was shown, along with blown-up portions showing the shoes, Groden was asked by plaintiffs' attorney Peter Gelblum if they changed his mind about the earlier photograph being a fake.
"No," he answered repeatedly. But later he said, "If I was able to authenticate these photographs it probably would (change his mind)."

The pictures were taken during a Buffalo Bills National Football League game on Sept. 26, 1993, the same game where Simpson was photographed wearing the Bruno Maglis by freelance photographer Harry Scull. That photograph appeared in the National Enquirer and was introduced earlier in the case.
The new photographs, one of which later appeared in a Buffalo Bills fan magazine, were taken by a different photographer.

Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of the June 12, 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. He is now battling a wrongful death civil lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.

Earlier, in arguing for the new photographs to be admitted into evidence, Daniel Petrocelli, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki he would authenticate them "through the defendant, no less, when we confront him with them." Simpson is due to take the witness stand later in the week when he is called by the defence.

During his first stint on the stand, which lasted two days, Simpson said under oath that he had never owned a pair of Bruno Maglis and never would own such "ugly" shoes. He also said Scull's photograph was a fake.
Petrocelli told the judge on Monday that in so testifying Simpson had taken "the risk of being caught red-handed," and that he intended to use the photographs to impeach him.

The new photographs, which came to light during the court's two-week holiday recess, were later passed around the jury box so panel members could examine them more closely. Defence lawyers had vigorously objected to the introduction of the photographs, saying it was "total sandbagging" because they had not been given copies by the plaintiffs.
Petrocelli said he received the photographs only on Saturday and Fujisaki ordered him to make them available to the defence.

Defence attorney Dan Leonard earlier asked Fujisaki to impose sanctions on the plaintiffs lawyers, charging they had broken the judge's "gag order" barring anyone connected with the case from talking to the media.

Leonard said a consultant to the plaintiffs' team, David Lipton, had appeared on the MSNBC television network talking about Groden. He also pointed out that Lipton was in the courtroom and asked that he be ejected.
After Gelblum said Lipton was not a consultant but had merely provided the plaintiffs' lawyers information on Groden, Fujisaki declined to impose sanctions but asked Lipton to leave the court.
